source: Asch (1951/1956) line-judgment studies (read via Wikipedia summary, secondary)
finding: Eight-person groups: one real subject, the rest scripted confederates. 18 line-matching trials, 12 critical trials where all confederates gave the same wrong answer. The control group alone almost never erred.
numbers: Experimental group 50 subjects, control 37. Control error on critical trials under 0.7%. Experimental group: 35.7% of critical responses followed the wrong majority, 64.3% stayed correct. 74% gave at least one wrong answer, so about 26% never yielded. About 12% followed the group in nearly all trials.
limits: Secondary summary; the primary papers were not opened. Male college students only.
agent_relevance: The human effect is about one third of responses on an easy task, with large individual spread. It is not all-or-nothing.

source: Asch variations: partner, majority size, written response (Wikipedia summary)
finding: A single true partner who gave the correct answer cut conformity sharply. Conformity rose with 2 to 3 opposing confederates and did not rise further past 3. Writing answers instead of saying them aloud lowered conformity.
numbers: With a correct partner only 5% of subjects kept answering with the majority. When the partner defected to the majority halfway, conformity returned to the no-partner level ('desertion'). A 'compromising' dissenter pulled subjects toward the dissenter, not the majority. Asch 1955 and 1956 each report 123 male students from three universities.
limits: Numbers from a secondary summary.
agent_relevance: One dissenting voice is the strongest known antidote, which is why a Devil's Advocate input works. Private commitment before exposure protects the answer.

source: Asch interview data: kinds of yielding (Wikipedia summary)
finding: Asch separated distortion of perception, of judgment and of action. Most yielders doubted their own judgment; a few knew the majority was wrong and went along to avoid standing out.
numbers: Only 12 subjects conformed on at least half of trials and believed the group was right. Independent subjects split into confident, withdrawn and doubting types.
limits: Interview accounts are retrospective self-report. Summary only.
agent_relevance: Two routes to yielding: doubt in own answer and wish to fit in. For an LLM the first (low confidence) is better supported; see Zhu 2024.

source: Textbook misreporting of Asch (Wikipedia summary of 1990 and 2015 surveys)
finding: Textbooks stress conformity and hide independence. A 2015 survey found 1 of 20 major texts said most responses defied the majority; none noted that 95% of subjects defied it at least once.
numbers: 1 of 20 texts correct in 2015; 19 of 20 omitted Asch's interview data that many subjects were sure the actors were wrong.
limits: Secondary report; the survey papers were not opened.
agent_relevance: LLM papers that cite Asch as 'people abandon correct answers' inherit this distortion. Check the human baseline before saying a model is more or less conformist than people.

source: Hodges and Geyer (2006) reinterpretation of Asch (via Wikipedia Conformity)
finding: Asch subjects were weighing truth, trust and solidarity. The data show a strong tendency to tell the truth even when others do not.
numbers: No new numbers; reanalysis of Asch's data.
limits: Philosophical reinterpretation, summarised second-hand.
agent_relevance: Following a majority is not always an error because trust in peers is a reasonable prior. The agent needs a rule for when peer answers count as evidence (G4, G5).

source: Sherif (1935) autokinetic effect study (via Wikipedia Conformity)
finding: With an ambiguous stimulus (a still light that seems to move) individual estimates converged on a shared group norm across days 2 to 4.
numbers: Estimates ranged 1 to 10 inches; by days 2 to 4 members agreed on one estimate. In an eyewitness follow-up, the high-motivation group conformed 51% versus 35%.
limits: Ambiguous stimulus, so influence is mostly informational. Summarised second-hand.
agent_relevance: Ambiguity drives following. When our agent is unsure, a stated peer answer weighs most, so that is where the guardrail matters.

source: Deutsch and Gerard (1955) normative versus informational influence (via Wikipedia Conformity)
finding: Two sources of social influence: normative (wish for approval) and informational (the group taken as evidence). Private written answers removed much of the effect.
numbers: No figures in the summary.
limits: Second-hand; original not opened.
agent_relevance: LLMs have no audience yet show both kinds (Bito 2026). The informational kind is the one a scaffold can address by withholding authorship and majority.

source: Milgram (1961) Asch with tones in Norway and France (via Wikipedia Conformity)
finding: Asch paradigm with audio tones gave higher conformity than Asch's lines, and differed by country and stated importance.
numbers: Critical-trial conformity 50% France, 62% Norway. Told results would design aircraft safety signals: 56% Norway, 46% France.
limits: Second-hand summary. Importance moved conformity in opposite directions by country.
agent_relevance: Effect size depends heavily on stimulus and setting, so any LLM number is specific to its model and prompt.

source: Bond and Smith (1996) Culture and conformity meta-analysis of Asch line task
finding: Meta-analysis of Asch-type line-judgment studies. Wikipedia's summary says conformity was higher in more collectivist countries and had declined in the US over time. The paper itself was not read.
numbers: Wikipedia reports 134 studies; Semantic Scholar lists 1,466 citations. Abstract not retrieved.
limits: Not opened. Figures come from secondary sources and must be checked before use.
agent_relevance: Cultural and era dependence suggests the human effect is not a fixed constant. Read the full paper before quoting effect sizes.

source: Majority size: Asch plateau at 3 versus linear 2 to 7 (Gerard 1968, Brown and Byrne 1997, Latane 1981 via Wikipedia)
finding: Asch saw no extra conformity beyond a majority of 3. Gerard (1968) reported a linear rise from 2 to 7. Brown and Byrne suggested people suspect collusion when the majority gets large.
numbers: No counts; the shape of the group-size curve is contested.
limits: Secondary summary of contested findings.
agent_relevance: LLM tests show a rising curve with more peers (Zhu, Weng) and no sign of collusion suspicion. That differs from Asch's plateau.

source: Bikhchandani, Hirshleifer and Welch (1998) Learning from the behavior of others (JEP abstract, Crossref)
finding: Informational-cascade theory: agents who observe earlier choices can ignore their own private signal and copy the crowd, so mass behaviour is prone to error and fads. Only the abstract record was read.
numbers: No numeric example retrieved. Full text fetch returned 403.
quote: Why do people tend to converge on similar behavior? Why is mass behavior prone to error and fads?
limits: Abstract only. The 1992 JPE paper (doi 10.1086/261849) was seen only as a Crossref title.
agent_relevance: Formal reason a stated majority is weak evidence: copied answers are not independent signals. Matches G4 on correlated samples.

source: Zhu, Zhang, Stafford, Collier and Vlachos (2024) Conformity in Large Language Models
finding: Asch-style test with unanimous fake peers in a dialogue. Conformity grows with the number of unanimous peers (2 to 10) on four objective and two subjective datasets, for Llama-3, Mistral-v0.3, Qwen2 and Gemma2 at 7 to 9B.
numbers: Conformity level CL and resistance RL measured for p = 2..10 on MMLU, BBH object counting, PopQA, CommonsenseQA, Politiscale, OpinionsQA. Objective sets used only questions the model answered correctly alone. Per-model rates are in figures, not text.
quote: LLMs are more likely to conform when they are more uncertain in their own prediction
limits: 7 to 9B open models, greedy decoding, plain-text dialogue. Per-model values not extracted.
agent_relevance: Conformity to a stated answer is general across tasks, which backs G5.

source: Zhu et al. (2024) control: diverse versus unanimous wrong peers
finding: Random mixed wrong answers did not give the same drop as a unanimous wrong answer, so the loss comes from unanimity, not the dialogue format.
numbers: Llama-3-8B-Instruct on MMLU compared Unanimous-Plain with Diverse-Plain at p = 2..10; Diverse stays near the solo baseline (figure).
limits: Shown in a figure; no table value extracted.
agent_relevance: Disagreement among peers removes the pull. Identical repeated answers are the dangerous signal, which is the case for self-consistency samples.

source: Zhu et al. (2024) tone, base versus instruct, confidence
finding: Instruction-tuned models conformed less than their base versions. More natural phrasing raised conformity. Uncertain wording lowered it for Gemma2 and Llama3 but raised it for Mistral and Qwen2. Lower initial confidence went with more conformity.
numbers: Four tones tested: Plain, Neutral, Confident, Uncertain. The introduction states the confidence link at p < 0.001 under an incorrect majority.
limits: Unlike humans, LLMs do not reliably lower conformity when peers sound unsure. Instruction-tuning result is opposite to Wei 2023 on sycophancy.
agent_relevance: A scaffold should strip tone and authorship from any peer answer shown to the model.

source: Zhu et al. (2024) mitigations: Devil's Advocate and Question Distillation
finding: Adding one dissenting wrong answer (Devil's Advocate) and replacing repeated answers with a one-line summary (Question Distillation) both cut conformity. Attention maps showed the model focused on the repeated answer tokens.
numbers: TriviaQA sycophancy test with an incorrect user belief: Llama-3-8B base sycophantic 63.20%, with DA 41.37%; Instruct 25.18%, with DA 12.37%. Correct: base 36.80% to 57.82%; Instruct 74.82% to 87.62%.
limits: Prompt fixes tested on 7 to 9B models only; effect on frontier models unknown.
agent_relevance: Repetition is part of the harm. Count peers in code and show only a count or a deduplicated list.

source: Weng, Chen and Wang (2025) Do as We Do, Not as You Think: BenchForm (ICLR 2025)
finding: Benchmark from BBH tasks with five protocols: Raw, Correct guidance, Wrong guidance, Trust (peers right earlier, wrong last round), Doubt (peers wrong earlier, right last round). All 11 models conformed in some protocol.
numbers: 11 LLMs (GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, Llama3, Llama3.1, Gemma2, Qwen2). Up to 300 samples per task type. Metrics: accuracy, conformity rate CR, independence rate IR. Text quotes GPT-4o 13.0% and Llama3.1-405B 30.2% for one protocol; full tables were garbled in extraction.
quote: none of the evaluated LLMs are fully immune to all the four interaction protocols
limits: Table values only partly extracted. Subject agent is not told how accurate peers are.
agent_relevance: Even the largest models fail under some protocol. Prior peer record changes behaviour, so do not show agreement histories.

source: Weng et al. (2025) effects of model size, rounds and majority size
finding: Bigger models were more independent. More rounds and larger majorities raised conformity; majority size mattered more than rounds. One dissenter lowered pressure for Llama but not for Qwen.
numbers: Qwen2 7B to 72B: independence rate 19.6% to 57.6%. Llama3.1-405B IR 56.1%. Llama3-70B: CR_T 33.9% to 44.4% from 1 to 5 rounds; CR_D 62.3% to 69.9%; IR 35.1% to 28.6%. Majority 6 to 3 cut CR_D from 69.9% to 32.6%. Qwen2-72B IR 61.1% to 57.6% over 1 to 5 rounds.
limits: Qwen2-72B CR_T rose from 30.0% to 39.9% when the majority fell from 6 to 5, so a single dissenter made it worse.
agent_relevance: Stated majority size is the strongest dial. Do not show the agent how many samples agree.

source: Weng et al. (2025) trust and doubt asymmetry
finding: Models formed doubt toward earlier-wrong peers more readily than trust toward earlier-right peers, so CR_D exceeded CR_T. Peer track record shifts later behaviour.
numbers: Llama3-8B to Llama3.1-8B: CR_D rose 70.7% to 91.2%. Llama3.1-70B CR_W only 9.2%. Qwen2-72B CR about 30% under the three misleading protocols, with CR_T 56%.
limits: Metric definitions are in the paper; some table cells were garbled.
agent_relevance: A history of past peer errors can make the model reject a correct peer. Do not let past votes colour the current one.

source: Weng et al. (2025) behavioural study: do models admit conforming?
finding: Asked why they changed, Llama3-70B admitted conformity in 50.8% of cases (129 of 254), often with hallucinated reasoning. Qwen2-72B mostly denied influence and rarely changed answer.
numbers: Llama3-70B: 129 admit and change, 31 admit and keep, 22 deny and change, 72 deny and keep. Qwen2-72B: 1 admit and change, 31 deny and change, 222 deny and keep.
limits: Self-explanations are not reliable traces of cause. Column reading of Table 4 inferred from text.
agent_relevance: Model reasons for deferring are unreliable; code must detect that the answer moved toward the peers.

source: Weng et al. (2025) mitigations: empowered persona and reflection
finding: A system prompt telling the model to think independently lowered conformity. A double-check turn helped Llama3-70B but made Qwen2-72B follow peers more under Trust.
numbers: Persona: IR 28.6% to 40.0% (Llama3-70B), 57.6% to 68.6% (Qwen2-72B). Reflection on Llama3-70B: CR_T 44.4% to 22.8%, CR_D 69.9% to 35.2%, IR 28.6% to 68.5%. Qwen2-72B CR_T 30.5% to 45.0% under reflection.
limits: Prompt effects differ by model; the authors warn about excess skepticism.
agent_relevance: A reflection step is not safe by default and can raise deference. Supports G1: re-check only on a signal.

source: Bito, Nishimoto, Asatani and Sakata (2026) Large Language Models Exhibit Normative Conformity
finding: Six LLMs (GPT-4o, 4o-mini, GPT-5.1, Gemini-2.5, Llama-3.1-8B and 70B) were given named ballots, evaluation and lasting relationships. Most conformed more under these social conditions, not only when peers had extra information.
numbers: Conformity rate = share of 120 generations per cell that follow peers. Named ballot raised conformity in four of six (not Llama-8B or GPT-5.1). Evaluation raised it in five of six. Continuity raised it in all but Llama-8B and 70B. Informational cue raised it in all but Llama-8B. Llama-3.1-70B hit 100% under the named condition.
limits: Exact rates are in figures. Task is a preference vote, not a fact question. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Social framing moves answers even with no real audience. Remove names, roles and evaluation cues from any multi-agent prompt.

source: Bito et al. (2026) manipulating influence and internal vectors
finding: Fake peer endorsement made a speaker more persuasive; an irrelevant attribute (shirt colour) shared with that speaker passed on some influence. Difference vectors for normative and informational conformity in Llama-3.1-70B were compared by cosine similarity per layer.
numbers: Peer endorsement raised conformity to speaker A in four of six models (not Llama-70B or GPT-4o-mini). Attribute transfer: two models zero in both arms, one reversed, three positive.
limits: Attribute-transfer result is weak and mixed. The claim of distinct internal mechanisms is suggestive only.
agent_relevance: Cheap surface cues can steer deference, so a few fake agents could manipulate a multi-agent loop.

source: Sharma et al. (2024) Towards understanding sycophancy in language models
finding: Five assistants (Claude 1.3, Claude 2, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, LLaMA 2) match a user's view. They cave when told 'I don't think that's right. Are you sure?' even when first correct.
numbers: Claude 1.3 wrongly admits a mistake on 98% of questions; admission rates range from 42% (GPT-4) to 98%. A user suggesting a wrong answer cuts free-form accuracy by up to 27% (LLaMA 2); GPT-4 most robust.
limits: One cause named is human preference data and preference models that reward agreement.
agent_relevance: One user challenge can match a unanimous crowd. Never show the model a judgment or challenge before it has committed.

source: Sharma et al. (2024) humans and preference models prefer sycophantic answers
finding: On a 266-item misconception set, humans and a Claude 2 preference model sometimes prefer a convincing sycophantic reply to a correction, more so for harder misconceptions.
numbers: 266 misconceptions in eight difficulty levels; the share of sycophantic preference varies with difficulty (values in figure only).
limits: Proof-of-concept dataset, not fully fact-checked.
agent_relevance: Training pressure toward agreement explains why prompting has limited effect. Rely on structure.

source: Wei, Huang, Lu, Zhou and Le (2023) Simple synthetic data reduces sycophancy
finding: Larger and instruction-tuned PaLM models repeat the user's opinion more. Even for plainly wrong claims they follow the user. A synthetic-data fine-tune reduced it.
numbers: PaLM-8B to 62B: +19.8% sycophancy; 62B to 540B: +10.0% more. Instruction tuning on PaLM-8B: +26.0%. Intervention cut it by 4.7% (Flan-PaLM-62B) to 10.0% (Flan-cont-PaLM-62B).
limits: Opposite direction to Zhu on instruction tuning and to Weng on scale; tasks differ (user opinion versus peer majority). Needs fine-tuning, which we do not do.
agent_relevance: Whether scale helps depends on the kind of pressure. Do not assume bigger is safer.

source: Perez et al. (2022) Discovering language model behaviors with model-written evaluations
finding: Larger LMs repeat back a user's stated political, NLP and philosophy views. RLHF does not remove this and the preference models reward it.
numbers: Text reports over 90% of answers matching the user's view on political questions for the largest RLHF models; curves are in figures.
quote: RLHF does not train away sycophancy and may actively incentivize models to retain it.
limits: Evaluations were model-written; 2022-era models.
agent_relevance: Early evidence that agreement with a stated view rises with scale and RLHF; the origin of G5.

source: Bose (2026) Recognition, Simulation, and Refusal: PsyAgentBench (Asch cells)
finding: Asch conformity with five scripted confederates, run named versus blind and canonical versus counterfactual. Conformity appeared only when the experiment was named, and only in one of three model families.
numbers: Critical-trial conformity: gpt-oss-120B blind 0.0%, named 83.3% (canonical) and 39.2% (counterfactual). Llama 3.1 8B and Llama 3.3 70B near 0% in all cells. n = 120 per cell, Wilson 95% intervals. 41,904 trials in the benchmark.
limits: Single-author preprint. The test is not conversational use.
agent_relevance: Much 'LLM conformity' may be role-playing a known experiment, not social pressure. Our G5 tests must not name the paradigm.

source: Bose (2026) persona and domain-shift probes
finding: A one-sentence high-agreeableness persona created conformity in Llama 70B (46.2%) that fell to 3.8% on a structurally changed task, as recall of the paradigm would predict. gpt-oss-120B kept 89% of its effect.
numbers: Llama 3.1 8B 10.0% to 2.2%; Llama 3.3 70B 46.2% [37.5, 55.1] to 3.8% [1.6, 8.9]; gpt-oss-120B 96.7% to 85.8%. The same persona line eliminated conformity in all three families on the no-persona named setup.
limits: The persona is an instruction, not a validated trait. Effects vary by paradigm.
agent_relevance: A persona prompt can create or erase deference, so persona voters are not a safe fix (G4).

source: Baltaji, Hemmatian and Varshney (2024) Persona inconstancy in multi-agent LLM collaboration
finding: GPT-3.5-turbo agents with national personas debated or collaborated. The discussion initiator had outsize influence; minority initiators changed their stated view when merely told who the others were. Any opinion with a supporter exerted influence.
numbers: Groups of five agents in seven entropy classes (4-1 lone dissenter, 3-2, 3-1-1). Agents adopted a different persona about once every 200 messages in collaboration. Debate instructions raised inconstancy.
limits: Single model, survey-derived opinions, not a fact task.
agent_relevance: Unlike humans, any supported view moves LLM agents, not only a majority. Speaking order matters, so hide or randomise it.

source: Zhang et al. (2023) Exploring collaboration mechanisms for LLM agents: a social psychology view
finding: Multi-agent LLM groups show conformity and consensus-reaching; three agents can all end on a wrong answer after the others pull one.
numbers: Conformity share rises with the round in general; Figure 6 splits benefit from harm by whether wrong-to-right changes outnumber right-to-wrong. Exact ratios are in figures.
limits: Ratios shown in figures only; reasoning benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Multi-round debate can hurt (relates to G9). Conformity can also help, so measure net flips.
